messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

The gravel truck’s brakes had failed on the winding coastal highway, and Javier remembered the sickening lurch as his sedan rolled three times. Metal screamed against asphalt, glass shattered inward like cold rain, and the steering column crushed against his chest. He lay trapped in the overturned cabin, breathing in the sharp tang of coolant and blood, while the driver’s anguished cries slowly faded into silence. In the weeks that followed, Javier found himself completely unable to put the event into words. The horror remained a heavy, wordless weight, surfacing not as a coherent story but as a sudden, high-pitched whine of tearing metal echoing in his head. Each time that auditory fragment surfaced, a wave of intense shame washed over him, leaving him staring at his hands as if they belonged to someone else. The relentless quality of those intrusions quickly forged new habits. Javier had come to believe that fighting the memories would only make them stronger, so he deliberately tried to leave his body, blanking out his mind the moment the metal-screeching started. He told himself that staying up until very late would keep the trauma at bay, and he forced himself to suppress thoughts of the crash, pushing his attention onto mundane studio tasks until his eyes burned with exhaustion. Paradoxically, the longer he resisted the experience, the more fragmented it became. His habit of suppressing thoughts only served to fracture the memory further, ensuring it would surface later as unprocessable noise rather than lived narrative. This relentless mental exhaustion eroded his sense of self, convincing him that he would never be able to feel normal emotions again and that the collision had occurred simply because he was the sort of man who brought ruin upon himself. That deepening conviction kept his nervous system permanently on high alert. Because he was certain he could not stop bad things from happening, his body prepared for the next disaster before it even arrived. He started scanning for exits the moment he stepped into any room, his eyes darting toward windows and doors instead of the faces of his students. When a colleague reached to tap his shoulder during rehearsal, Javier reacted with alarm, his body flinching as if another collision were imminent. The constant hypervigilance, in turn, fed directly back into his psychological landscape. The sustained fear and scanning never gave his mind a moment to rest, which meant the traumatic fragments were never properly processed and kept returning with fresh intensity. Worse, the relentless negative emotions his own body produced began to confirm his worst fears, cementing his belief that he was fundamentally powerless and that his emotional capacity was permanently broken. These cycles finally caught up with his livelihood. Javier had spent thirty years choreographing and teaching Latin dance, but the studio now felt like a gauntlet. He could not allow his dancers to make contact during lifts, nor could he stand in the center of a packed room without fixating on the double doors behind him. Elena watched as her husband withdrew into a quiet, exhausted version of himself, skipping meals and avoiding the very profession that had defined his life. He finally sought help not because the memories had lessened, but because the weight of waiting for the next disaster had made it impossible to teach, to love, or to simply breathe. He was ready to stop running from the crash, hoping someone could show him how to feel like himself again without feeling the need to leave his body or stay awake until dawn.
